findings.title: SpanFlusher.join breaks out of the loop on timeout, leaving later flusher processes un-terminated
findings.body: join() sets `stopped`, computes a single `deadline`, calls `self.next_step.join(timeout)`, and then iterates processes. For every process it first checks `if remaining_time <= 0: break`, which exits the whole loop before the `while ... is_alive()` wait and before `process.terminate()` for that and all remaining processes. Because `next_step.join(timeout)` is called on the line above with the same full timeout, it can consume the entire budget on its own, so in the worst case *no* worker process is ever terminated. The per-process `terminate()` was the only safety net for a worker that is hung inside `flush_segments`/`produce` and therefore never observes the shared `stopped` flag; with this break, such hung spawn processes keep running (holding Redis/Kafka connections, and potentially still producing) after the consumer has moved on via rebalance. Use `continue`/per-process termination instead of `break`, and terminate all processes that exceed the deadline rather than skipping them.

findings.title: Added `time.sleep(0.1)` is a no-op because `time.sleep` is monkeypatched, so the flusher race is not actually fixed
findings.body: test_basic begins with `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`, which replaces `time.sleep` on the `time` module. The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` (with the comment 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change') therefore calls the patched lambda and sleeps for zero seconds, so it provides no delay or yield. The line was clearly intended to let the background flusher thread observe `current_drift.value = 9000` before `step.join()` sets `stopped` and the thread exits; since no real waiting happens, the race remains and the test can intermittently observe an empty `messages` list. Restore real sleeping for this call (e.g. keep a reference to the original `time.sleep` and use it, or synchronize explicitly on the flusher having flushed) or the extra line gives false confidence.

findings.title: Restarting a hung flusher in thread mode leaves the old thread running
findings.body: In `_ensure_processes_alive`, a process detected as dead/hung is only killed when `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. When `produce_to_pipe` is set (the code uses `threading.Thread` instead of a spawn process, as done by the tests), the old thread is neither stopped nor joined before `_create_process_for_shards` overwrites `self.processes[process_index]` with a brand-new thread. Both threads then run `SpanFlusher.main` for the same shards concurrently, producing the same flushed segments twice and racing on `done_flush_segments`/Redis key deletion. This is limited to the thread path, but that path is what the test suite relies on, and a hang-triggered restart there would corrupt results.

findings.title: Non-positive `max_processes` silently disables the flusher or spawns one process per shard
findings.body: `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` (and `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(...))`) does no validation. Passing `--flusher-processes 0` is treated as falsy and becomes `len(assigned_shards)` (i.e. 'max 0' spawns one process per shard), while a negative value makes `num_processes = min(negative, n)` negative, so `range(self.num_processes)` is empty, `process_to_shards_map`/`processes`/`buffers` are all empty, and no flusher worker is ever created. In that state `submit()` still inserts spans into Redis and forwards to `next_step`, but nothing ever calls `flush_segments`, so segments are never expired or produced and Redis grows without bound — with no error or warning. Validate that `max_processes >= 1` (or explicitly define the meaning of 0) rather than relying on `or`.

findings.title: `_create_process_for_shard` is dead code and never called
findings.body: `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is defined but no caller exists; the restart path in `_ensure_processes_alive` calls `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` directly. This unused method adds confusion about whether a single-shard restart path is supposed to exist (it would also break the assumption that a process owns a fixed set of shards) and should be removed.

findings.title: New multiprocess flusher is only checked structurally, not for actual flushing or restart behavior
findings.body: test_flusher_processes_limit only asserts the sizes of `processes`/`process_to_shards_map` and then calls `step.join()`; it runs in thread mode (`produce_to_pipe`) and never submits spans, so it never verifies that spans for different partitions are actually flushed/produced by the correct per-shard processes, nor does it exercise `_ensure_processes_alive` (dead/hung restart) or the per-process backpressure accounting. The core new behavior (each process flushing its own shards and restarting independently) has no functional test coverage.
